approved: Employment, Skills, Small and Family Business

The majority voted in favour of keeping unchanged the usual [second reading motion](https://peo.gov.au/understand-our-parliament/how-parliament-works/bills-and-laws/making-a-law-in-the-australian-parliament/), which is "*that the bill be read a second time*" (parliamentary jargon for agreeing with the main idea of the bill). This question was put after Gorton MP [Brendan O'Connor](https://theyvoteforyou.org.au/people/representatives/gorton/brendan_o'connor) (Labor) moved an amendment that would have removed all the words after 'that' and replaced them with other words (see below). ### Amendment text > *That all words after "That" be omitted with a view to substituting the following words:* > > *"whilst not declining to give the bill a second reading, the House expresses concerns over deficiencies in the bill, including the:* > > *(1) lack of certainty that the measure will lower payment times;* > > *(2) light treatment of supply chain financing; and* > > *(3) ability for businesses to hide extremely long payment times to small businesses".*

The Payment Times Reporting (Consequential Amendments) Bill 2020 was introduced to amend the *Taxation Administration Act 1953*, enabling the Commissioner of Taxation to disclose certain tax information to the Payment Times Reporting Regulator for administering the new reporting framework.

The speaker moved to amend the Payment Times Reporting Bill 2020, expressing concerns that it lacks certainty to lower payment times, inadequately addresses supply chain financing, and allows businesses to hide extremely long payment times to small businesses. Labor supports the bill as a first step but will refer it to a Senate committee for further inquiry.

Speaking on the Payment Times Reporting Bill, noted Australia's GDP fell 0.3 per cent in the March quarter, ending a 29-year run without recession, and said this was about a sixth of the average OECD decline, with China's GDP falling almost 10 per cent, while the OECD forecast Australia's recovery would be third-best among member nations behind South Korea and Turkey.

Labor supported the Payment Times Reporting Bill 2020 as a first step but argued it is insufficient, calling for a Senate inquiry to consider mandating 30-day payment times for large businesses to small suppliers, penalties for late payments, and better regulator resourcing, citing the EU and New Zealand as examples.

The member for Dobell announced Labor's support for the Payment Times Reporting Bill 2020 as a first step, but argued it should be referred to the Senate economics legislation committee for inquiry over concerns including the lack of mandated 30‑day payment times, no penalties for late payments, and insufficient reporting on supply chain financing.

The speaker supported the Payment Times Reporting Bill 2020 and its consequential amendments as a first step, but argued the legislation is a weak measure relying on self-regulation rather than tough penalties to address late payments and supply chain financing fees harming small businesses.

The Payment Times Reporting Bill 2020 is a step forward but insufficient, as late payments by large businesses cost Australian SMEs $7 billion annually and voluntary codes have failed; the speaker called for stronger regulation, including mandated 30-day payment terms and a Senate inquiry into systemic reforms.

The Payment Times Reporting Bill 2020 will increase transparency on payment times and practices, incentivising faster payments to small businesses, as seen when Rio Tinto and Telstra revised policies after public exposure; the speaker opposed legislated payment times, arguing they could delay payments, and noted government support including $50,000 cashback and JobKeeper for small businesses.
How did each party vote on the Payment Times Reporting (Consequential Amendments) Bill 2020?
